title: Little words at the end of the sentence
goal: Master a group of words with no dictionary meaning that still set the whole mood of a sentence — the tone of voice, written down.
bekal: using *thì* to highlight the topic of a sentence
hearing the difference between a correct sentence and one that sounds like a real person

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Đi ăn trưa
dialogs.intro: Midday on campus. This conversation is deliberately packed with little end-of-sentence words — count how many you find before reading the notes.

notes: **These words have no dictionary meaning — they carry attitude.** English does the same job with tone of voice and add-ons like "…, OK?", "…, isn't it?", "you know", "just", "come on". Vietnamese packs it into one small syllable at the end. Don't look for a translation; listen for the mood.

**Dropping them all makes your sentences correct but cold.** *Đi ăn trưa.* is a flat command; *Đi ăn trưa nhé?* is a warm invitation. Both are grammatical. The difference is the one between "Go eat lunch." and "Shall we grab lunch?" — and it's a big one.

**Ạ is the only one that's nearly required.** To anyone older, to staff, to teachers, and to anyone you address as *anh*, *chị*, *cô*, *chú*, *bác*, *ông*, *bà* — add *ạ* at the end. It can't be translated; it just raises the politeness level, and its absence is noticed at once.

**Nhé and nhỉ sound alike but point in opposite directions.** *Nhé* suggests something and asks agreement to an **action**: *Đi nhé?* ("shall we go?"). *Nhỉ* seeks agreement on a **shared impression**: *Ngon nhỉ?* ("tasty, isn't it?"). One invites you along, the other invites you to agree.

**Thì highlights the topic of a sentence**, much like "as for …": *Em thì không ăn cay được.* = "as for me, I can't eat spicy food". It's used when you want to contrast yourself with what was just mentioned — here, Linh, who loves spice.

**Cơ is a gentle whine**, and one of the most typically northern Vietnamese words: *Em hết tiền rồi cơ.* = "I'm out of money, ugh". It feels a bit pouty, a bit complaining, and young people use it a lot. In the south you'll hardly hear it.

grammars.title: Ten little words and their English feel
body: This table is the heart of the unit. Read the "English feel" column: none of them is a translation, just the tone the word adds.

rows: turning a statement into a question

after: ⚠️ **Don't stack more than two.** *Đi nhé!* and *Đi thôi nhé!* are natural; stacking three or four makes you sound like you're doing an impression. One little word is enough to change the mood.
The order when there are two: the limiting one first, the inviting one last — *thôi nhé*, *rồi đấy*, *thôi ạ*. At A1 just use one; the second will come by itself once you've listened enough.

grammars.title: One sentence, eight moods
body: The basic sentence stays the same: *Đi ăn phở* — "go eat phở". Only the ending changes, and the whole meaning changes with it.
after: Read all eight lines aloud, in order, and notice that **your tone of voice changes by itself** to follow the little word. That's no accident: these words store the tone of speech, which is why you can't learn them from a list without saying them.
⚠️ Don't confuse ***đi* at the end of a sentence** ("go on!, come on") with ***đi* before a verb** ("go"). *Đi ăn phở đi!* has both, and it's a sentence people really say.

blocks.text: *Thì* goes **after** the part you want to highlight, and marks that what follows is a comment about it. The English feel is "as for …" or a stressed word.

head: Tiếng Việt
Say it
Meaning
rows: Em thì không ăn cay được.
Em thì không ăn kay dượk.
As for me, I can't eat spicy food.
The phở is good, but expensive.
Tiếng Việt thì khó, nhưng hay.
Tiếng Việt thì khó, nyưng hay.

blocks.text: ⚠️ *Thì* has a second job as "then" in conditional sentences — *Nếu trời mưa **thì** ở nhà.* ("if it rains, then stay home"). That's for unit 18. Position tells them apart: *thì* after a noun highlights the topic; *thì* after a clause means "then".
Little end-of-sentence words show up most in exactly the sentences you'll need most: congratulating, wishing well, and saying goodbye.

Chúk ang một ngày tốt làng nyé!

blocks.title: Cố lên — the two words Vietnamese people say to friends most often
items: Literally "try up", it means "you can do it!", "go for it!". It's said to anyone facing an exam, hard work or a bad day — and it's meant sincerely, not as a mere formality.
If you're learning Vietnamese and say it to a Vietnamese person, be ready: *Cố lên!* from a foreigner almost always gets a big smile and, soon after, an invitation to eat together.
